'''Alexander Marson''' (born June 5, 1979) is an American [[biologist]] and infectious disease doctor who specializes in [[genetics]], human [[immunology]], and [[Genome editing|genome engineering]]. He is the director of the [[Gladstone Institutes| Gladstone-UCSF Institute of Genomic Immunology]],<ref>{{Cite web|title=Two New Research Institutes in the Bay Area|url=https://gladstone.org/news/two-new-research-institutes-bay-area|website=gladstone.org|access-date=2020-05-12}}</ref> and a tenured professor with a dual appointment in the Department of Medicine and the Department of Microbiology & Immunology at the [[University of California, San Francisco]] (UCSF).<ref name=":2">{{Cite web|url=https://marsonlab.ucsf.edu/|title=Welcome {{!}} Marson Laboratory|website=marsonlab.ucsf.edu|access-date=2019-02-27}}</ref>

Marson is best known for his work with [[CRISPR|Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats]] (CRISPR), particularly for his advances in furthering understanding of the genomics of human [[T cell]] function.<ref name=wired>{{Cite magazine|url=https://www.wired.com/story/wired25-sean-parker-alex-marson-crispr-dna-programming/|title=Why DNA Is the Most Exciting Programming Language Today|last=Molteni|first=Megan|date=2018-09-18|magazine=Wired|access-date=2019-02-27|issn=1059-1028}}</ref> Marson also holds affiliations with the [[Parker Institute for Cancer Immunotherapy]] (PICI), the [[Chan Zuckerberg Biohub]],<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=https://www.ucsf.edu/news/2017/02/405746/15-ucsf-researchers-named-first-cohort-chan-zuckerberg-biohub-investigators|title=15 UCSF Researchers Named to First Cohort of Chan Zuckerberg Biohub Investigators|website=UC San Francisco|language=en|access-date=2019-02-27}}</ref> and the [[Innovative Genomics Institute]] (IGI).

==Biography==
Alex Marson was born June 5, 1979, in Manhattan, New York. He is the son of Ellen Marson, a professor of Spanish literature and former director of [[Hadassah Women's Zionist Organization of America|Hadassah]], and Bernard Marson, an architect.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1989/08/17/garden/family-decorating-living-room-last.html|title=Family Decorating: Living Room Last|last=Lawson|first=Carol|date=1989-08-17|work=The New York Times|access-date=2019-03-14|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331}}</ref> Marson graduated [[summa cum laude]] with an A.B. in biology from [[Harvard University]] in 2001. He then pursued a master's degree in Biological Sciences from the [[University of Cambridge]] in 2003. Later, he received a Ph.D. in Biology from [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] in 2008.

Marson's research focuses on reprogramming human immune cells, especially T cells, with CRISPR.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Alexander Marson - Google Scholar Citations|url=https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=M3Vi46UAAAAJ&hl=en|website=scholar.google.com|access-date=2020-05-29}}</ref> The applications of this research are in the [[Cancer treatment|treatment of cancer]], [[autoimmune disease]]s, [[HIV]] and a wide range of other diseases. In August 2018, Marson was selected as [[Wired (magazine)|Wired Magazine]]'s 25 Icons of the next 25 Years for his research in DNA programming and genome editing for cancer immunotherapy.<ref name=wired/>

In April & May 2020, Marson and colleagues at UCSF, the [[Gladstone Institutes]], & UC Berkeley collaborated on the meta-testing of COVID-19 antibody tests to verify the accuracy of results.<ref>{{Cite news|author=Apoorva Mandavilli|author-link=Apoorva Mandavilli|date=2020-04-24|title=Coronavirus Antibody Tests: Can You Trust the Results?|language=en-US|work=The New York Times|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2020/04/24/health/coronavirus-antibody-tests.html|access-date=2020-05-01|issn=0362-4331}}</ref> Marson appeared on CNN,<ref>{{Cite tweet |title=Out of 12 antibody tests that were studied by the COVID-19 Testing Project, one gave false positives more than 15% of the time. Three other tests gave false positives more than 10% of the time. https://cnn.it/35gMhMB pic.twitter.com/gdCKgUH1s5|number=1255714534171586561|date=2020-04-29|access-date=2020-05-01|user=CNNTonight}}</ref> PBS,<ref>{{Cite web|title=Why antibody tests, a crucial step toward overcoming COVID-19, are still unreliable|url=https://www.pbs.org/newshour/show/why-antibody-tests-a-crucial-step-toward-overcoming-covid-19-are-still-unreliable|date=2020-04-29|website=PBS NewsHour|language=en-us|access-date=2020-05-01}}</ref> NBC,<ref>{{Cite web|title=Congress sounds alarm over inaccurate antibody tests|url=https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/congress/congress-sounds-alarm-over-inaccurate-antibody-tests-n1194876|website=NBC News|language=en|access-date=2020-05-29}}</ref> and NPR.<ref>{{Cite web|title=A Double-Barreled Approach To Antibody Testing Could Improve Accuracy|url=https://www.npr.org/sections/health-shots/2020/05/20/859688631/a-double-barreled-approach-to-antibody-testing-could-improve-accuracy|website=NPR.org|language=en|access-date=2020-05-29}}</ref>

Marson is the scientific director for biomedicine at the Innovative Genomics Institute (IGI).<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://innovativegenomics.org/news/alex-marson-appointed-igi-scientific-director-of-biomedicine/|title=Alex Marson Appointed IGI Scientific Director of Biomedicine|date=2018-07-11|website=Innovative Genomics Institute (IGI)|language=en-US|access-date=2019-03-14}}</ref> He is a member of the Parker Institute for Cancer Immunotherapy and was selected as one of the inaugural Chan Zuckerberg Biohub investigators.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.czbiohub.org/people3/investigators/|title=Investigator Program – Chan Zuckerberg Biohub|language=en-US|access-date=2019-03-14|archive-date=2021-04-20|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210420195553/https://www.czbiohub.org/people3/investigators/|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite web|url=https://www.parkerici.org/person/alexander-marson-md-phd/|title=Alexander Marson, MD, PhD|website=Parker Institute for Cancer Immunotherapy|language=en-US|access-date=2019-03-14}}</ref>
